## Why measure code at all?

Two solutions can both be *correct* and still be worlds apart. One finds an answer in milliseconds on a million items; the other would still be running next week. Interviews — and production systems — care about the second axis: **cost**.

We measure cost in two currencies:

- **Time** — how many steps the algorithm takes as input grows
- **Space** — how much extra memory it needs as input grows

The key phrase is *as input grows*. We don't care that your laptop runs something in 3 ms. We care about the **shape of the growth curve**.

## Big-O: the vocabulary of growth

Big-O notation describes the **upper bound** of that growth curve, keeping only the dominant term and dropping constants.

| Big-O | Name | Mental model |
|---|---|---|
| O(1) | Constant | Grab one item from a known shelf |
| O(log n) | Logarithmic | Halve the search space each step |
| O(n) | Linear | Look at every item once |
| O(n log n) | Linearithmic | Sort's natural habitat |
| O(n²) | Quadratic | Compare every pair |
| O(2ⁿ) | Exponential | Try every subset — danger zone |

If you remember one ranking, remember this one. In interviews, moving an answer one row *up* this table is usually the whole game.

content.caption: Same problem, two growth curves

content.md: **Drop constants, keep the dominant term.** O(2n + 10) is just O(n). O(n² + n) is just O(n²). Big-O is about the *shape* at scale, not the exact step count.

## Space complexity and a word on "amortized"

Space complexity counts **extra** memory your algorithm allocates — the input itself is free. `hasDuplicateFast` above is O(n) space because the set can grow to hold every element; the slow version is O(1) space. That's the classic **time ↔ space trade-off**, and you'll make it deliberately all course long.

One more word you'll meet: **amortized**. A dynamic array (like a JavaScript array) occasionally doubles its capacity — an expensive O(n) moment — but spread across all the cheap appends, the *average* push is O(1). We say push is *amortized O(1)*. The occasional spike is paid for by the many cheap operations around it.

## Guided example: analyzing Two Sum

Let's analyze a real interview classic end to end. **Problem:** given an array `nums` and a `target`, return the indices of two numbers that add up to `target`.

### Attempt 1 — brute force

The most direct idea: try every pair.

content.caption: Attempt 1 — every pair, O(n²) time, O(1) space

content.md:
Count the work: the outer loop runs n times, the inner loop up to n times for each — about n²/2 comparisons. Dropping the constant ½: **O(n²) time**. No extra memory: **O(1) space**.

### Attempt 2 — ask a better question

Walking through the array, for each number `x` we don't need to *search* for a partner — we need to know: **"have I already seen `target − x`?"** A hash map answers that in O(1).

content.caption: Attempt 2 — one pass with a map, O(n) time, O(n) space

content.md: **The pattern behind the pattern.** We didn't get faster by clever micro-optimization — we *restructured the question* so a data structure could answer it instantly. That single move (trade O(n) memory to kill an inner loop) reappears in dozens of problems you'll meet.

questions.explanation: Two nested loops, each running n times → n × n = n² increments.
Big-O drops constant factors and lower-order terms: 3n + 20 grows linearly, so O(n).

questions.prompt: An algorithm halves its search space on every step. Its time complexity is…
questions.explanation: Repeated halving reaches 1 in log₂(n) steps — the signature of binary search.

questions.prompt: hasDuplicateFast uses a Set that may hold every input element. Its SPACE complexity is…
questions.explanation: Extra memory grows linearly with input size — the set can hold all n elements.

questions.prompt: JavaScript array push is 'amortized O(1)' because…
options: every push is exactly one step
occasional expensive resizes average out across many cheap pushes
questions.explanation: Capacity doubling is O(n) occasionally, but spread over all pushes the average cost per push is constant.

## Practice

The in-browser problem workspace (editor, test runner, submissions) ships with the Practice engine. Until then, this lesson is a free pass — mark it complete and keep moving.

When problems land here, this chapter's set will be:

1. **Contains Duplicate** — apply the time/space trade-off you just learned
2. **Two Sum** — the guided example, now hands-on
3. **Valid Anagram** — frequency counting warm-up
Solved problems will enter your spaced-repetition queue automatically (1 → 3 → 7 → 14 → 30 days).

## Chapter checkpoint

Before moving on, you should be able to answer these without looking:

- What does Big-O actually describe? *(the growth **shape** of cost as input scales — constants dropped)*
- Rank these fastest-growing last: O(n log n), O(1), O(2ⁿ), O(n), O(log n), O(n²)
- Why is `hasDuplicateFast` O(n) **space**? What did it buy us?
- What does *amortized* O(1) mean for array push?

If any of these feel shaky, skim the theory lesson once more — the rest of the course leans on this vocabulary constantly.
**Habit to build now:** after every problem you ever solve, state its time and space complexity out loud. In interviews this is expected unprompted.
